Vasectomy is an effective, safe, and cost-effective option for permanent contraception with a failure rate of <1%, complication rate of 1% to 2%, and cost range of US$350-1,000.
Around 10% of couples using contraception choose vasectomy.

Candidates for the procedure are males interested in permanent contraception, especially those who are older than 30 years and in a stable relationship. Patients who request reversal of the vasectomy are more likely to be younger men, have partners who work outside the home, and have a change in marital status following vasectomy.
Any illness or injury that would supersede an elective procedure.
Presence of a scrotal hematoma, active genitourinary or groin infection, or sperm granuloma that impedes vas isolation.

Consider urologic consultation in patients with a history of solitary testicle, extensive genital surgery, anatomic abnormalities (such as a nonpalpable vas deferens, varicocele, hydrocele, cryptorchidism, or scrotal mass), or a bleeding diathesis.

Perform preoperative consultation. Discuss history of abnormalities in sexual development, bleeding disorders, genital injury, and genitourinary surgery in addition to a complete genital examination with focus to confirm a single vas deferens and testicle on each side and absence of anatomic abnormalities.

Diazepam 10 mg orally or other benzodiazepines can be administered approximately one hour prior for anxiolysis and relaxation of the scrotal and cremasteric muscles. Consider an additional dose immediately prior to the procedure.
Warm the room (70-80 degrees F) to help relax the cremasteric and the scrotal muscles.
A study randomized 316 men undergoing vasectomy to EMLA cream or no topical anesthesia applied 1 hour prior to the procedure. The study found no difference in pain scores.
To block the vasal nerve, local anesthesia can be applied with an external spermatic sheath injection or with a no-needle jet injection technique.

A randomized controlled trial of 50 patients had statistically significant improvement in pain from anesthetic administration with no-needle vasectomy compared with needle injection, with no statistically significant difference in intraoperative pain between the two techniques.

listitem.strong: Steps in the No-Scalpel Vasectomy Procedure

list.listitem: Position the vas under the anesthesia wheal using the three-finger technique. Use a vas fixation ring clamp to gently entrap the vas and a minimal amount of overlying tightly stretched scrotal skin.

Create a skin opening of ≤10 mm by piercing the skin with the dissecting forceps followed by gently spreading the tissue overlying the vas to expose the bare anterior wall of the vas. Take care not to go through the vas.

To elevate the vas through the incision, one of two methods can be applied: Pierce or grasp the bare vas with one tip of the dissecting forceps and then use a supinating motion to elevate the vas. Grasp the vas with a different vas ring clamp. The vas can also be elevated through the opening with an Allis clamp or towel clamp.
Dissect perivasal tissue until a bare 2 cm vas loop is isolated. The vas ring clamp can be repositioned at any time for optimal dissection.
During dissection, exercise care to avoid trauma to the perivasal (pampiniform) blood vessels. Gauze may be used to achieve finer blunt dissection.
The tip of a hemostat or tips of the dissecting forceps can be inserted into the window of the vas deferens loop and gently spread to completely isolate the vas.
Secure the vas loop ends with straight or curved hemostats prior to excision and end occlusion.

The vas is divided and a segment of vas is removed. The minimum length that needs be removed to prevent recanalization and possible failure is controversial. Recanalization rates more likely reflect occlusion technique used than the length of vas segment removed. The preferred method to avoid recanalization and possible vasectomy failure is vasal end cautery with fascial interposition. Typically, remove at least 10 mm to 15 mm, but this varies in practice between 0 cm to 5 cm.

If a segment is removed, it can be sent for histological examination. However, routine pathological confirmation is not required. Pathologic documentation that full-thickness vas was excised can be helpful in the event of vasectomy failure.
Bedrest is recommended for the first 24 hours; maintain dressing and scrotal support for 48 to 72 hours.
Pain management with intermittent ice pack and over-the-counter pain medications.
Sexual activity and ejaculation should be avoided for one week and alternative forms of contraception should be used until confirmation of sterility.
Intraoperative and early postoperative pain, bleeding, and infection rates are primarily related to the method of vas isolation.
Vas isolation can be achieved using a conventional vasectomy (utilizing a scalpel) or a minimally-invasive vasectomy (no scalpel) that has lower complication rates.

listitem.strong: Disruption and occlusion of the vas

list.listitem: Vas occlusion is the main contributor to vasectomy success rates.
Simple suture ligation with excision is less effective due to likely spontaneous recanalization secondary to vasal end ischemic necrosis and sloughing.
Ligation and excision have high failure rates (1%-6%) and should not be the sole method of vasal disruption.
Cautery may be combined with excision of a vas segment, folding back, or fascial interposition.
Thermal cautery or electrocautery of the vas lumen is more effective than ligation and excision alone.
Fulguration using a battery-powered handheld cautery device scars and occludes the vas lumen more effectively than electrocautery.

At Marie Stopes International health centers (multinational family planning clinics where 100,000 vasectomies have been performed worldwide), use of intraluminal cautery without separation of the vasa has a reported failure rate of less than 1 percent.

A small study of 106 men evaluated flushing the prostatic end of the vas deferens with 10 mL of normal saline and found it was effective in removing sperm from the distal vas but did not increase the rate of azoospermia. Similar results were seen in other randomized trials.
Fascial interposition (burying one vasal end within the internal spermatic fascia) significantly reduces vasectomy failure compared with no fascial interposition (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.26-0.70).

Cautery plus fascial interposition is more effective than ligation and excision plus fascial interposition (failure rate of 0.3% vs. 8.7%, OR 37, 95% CI 12-116).
A study of 6248 patients showed thermal cautery of both ends and fascial interposition had no treatment failures and low complication rates.
Open-ended vasectomy leaves the testicular end of the divided vas unoccluded and occludes the abdominal/prostatic end. Fascial interposition is typically used in addition to prevent recanalization.

Scrotal closure can be accomplished with clips, clamps, sutures, or cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive. The incision may also be left open to heal by secondary intention with limited data comparing these methods.
Perioperative bleeding occurs in 2.4% of no-scalpel vasectomies and 4.0% of conventional vasectomies, whereas hematoma occurs in 2.4% of no-scalpel vasectomies and 12.5% of conventional vasectomies.
Postoperative infection occurs in 0.7% of no-scalpel vasectomies and 2.2% of conventional vasectomies.
Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for routine vasectomy, but consider in patients with a high risk of post-operative infection.

Post-vasectomy pain syndrome, incidence between 1% to 6%, is persistent or recurrent scrotal pain that occurs months to years after vasectomy and can be treated conservatively with over-the-counter pain medications. Local nerve blocks or steroid injections can be performed in refractory cases.
A case series of 13 patients with post-vasectomy pain syndrome reported reported that all but one had relief of pain after vasovasostomy (reversal).
Most studies report a failure rate (defined as lack of azoospermia on semen analysis or presence of pregnancy) of <1%.

When confirming sterility, evidence from 56 studies recommended using a protocol with 1 test showing azoospermia 3 months and 20 ejaculations post-vasectomy. The studies found a median of greater than 80% of patients achieved azoospermia with this protocol. In the same review, a small percentage of patients (1.4%) demonstrated persistent presence of nonmotile sperm with a portion eventually achieving azoospermia.
Time to azoospermia decreases with increasing number of ejaculations and coital frequency following vasectomy and increases with patient age.

The British Andrology Society recommends that patients with presence of persistent nonmotile sperm on post-vasectomy semen analysis undergo monthly follow-up samples until one test demonstrates azoospermia or two consecutive tests demonstrate low numbers of nonmotile sperm (<100,000 per mL) and seven months have elapsed since vasectomy.

The American Urologic Association guidelines state that patients may stop using other methods of contraception when examination of one well-mixed, uncentrifuged, fresh post-vasectomy semen specimen shows azoospermia or only rare nonmotile sperm (defined as presence of ≤100,000 nonmotile sperm/mL based on microscopic exam of at least 50 high-powered fields).

A qualitative home test has been developed that can accurately detect sperm counts <250,000 per mL. It was found to have a positive predictive value of 93% and a negative predictive value of 97% in a cohort of 144 post-vasectomy semen samples. However, it is not yet supported by clinical trials or current guidelines to confirm sterility.
A secondary analysis of over 3,200 semen samples showed microscopic examination of uncentrifuged specimens is a reliable method for identifying semen samples after vasectomy.
Recanalization and pregnancy following vasectomy are rare (0.4% and 0.07%, respectively).
Vasectomy reversal involves reanastomosis (vasovasostomy) of the vas deferens with 50% to 70% success rate. Rates decline with increasing time between vasectomy and reversal.
Time since vasectomy (less than 15 years) and age of female partner (less than 40 years) increase rates of success.
A study of 206 men found that those with increased follicle-stimulating hormone had an increased likelihood of needing assisted reproduction to achieve pregnancy after vasectomy reversal.

An absorbable stent placement for vasectomy reversal was found to be inferior to 2-layer microscopic vasovasostomy in achieving pregnancy (RR of conception in stent group: 0.42 [0.24-0.71, p = 0.002]).
Patients may require a more complicated procedure called a vasoepididymostomy; there are several models used to help identify these patients.
Studies have shown no measurable association between vasectomy and malignancy of the prostate or testes.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 observational studies with nearly 300,000 participants found no statistically significant association between vasectomy and cardiovascular disease. A subsequent meta-analysis of 53 observational studies with over 2.5 million participants reached the same conclusion.
Patient education materials: see https://www.aafp.org/afp/2006/1215/p2076.html
